units.title: Literary Works
units.intro: Grammar: a review of subordination (subordinate clauses) and lexical cohesion through collocation.

cards.title: Subordination
rule: A **subordinate clause** cannot stand alone; it depends on a main clause. It starts with a **subordinator**: time (*when, while, after, before, until*), reason (*because, since, as*), contrast (*although, though, whereas*), condition (*if, unless*), purpose (*so that*), relative (*who, which, that*).
Comma rule: when the subordinate clause comes **first**, use a comma: ***Although the novel is long,** it is exciting.*

examples.text: Because the story was sad, many readers cried.
Although he was poor. He was happy.
examples.fix: Although he was poor, he was happy.

examples.text: She read the poem until she understood it.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: The manager rejected the proposal because he felt that ________ details were provided to support the budget.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** The blank modifies the noun 'details'. 'Details' is a plural countable noun (indicated by the '-s' ending).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Uncountable quantifiers like 'little' and 'a little' cannot modify plural countable nouns. 'Too few' is the correct quantifier for countable nouns in a negative context.
Tigrinya speakers often conflate 'few' and 'little' as both translate to 'ውሑድ' or 'ቅሩብ'.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: Which of the following sentences contains a pluralization error?

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** 'Crisis' is a noun of Greek origin.
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** National exams frequently test irregular non-English plurals.

cards.answer: The school board discussed several educational crisises.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Although the construction project has been delayed, ________ progress has been made this week.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
'Progress' is an uncountable noun in English. It cannot be pluralized and cannot pair with countable quantifiers.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
'A few' and 'many' are strictly countable. 'Few' is also countable. 'Some' can modify both countable and uncountable nouns, making it the only grammatically viable option here.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Progress' (ዕብየት/ምስጓም) ዘይቝጸር ስም (uncountable noun) እዩ። 'Many' ን 'a few' ን ንዝቝጸሩ ስማት ጥራይ ስለ ዝኾኑ ምስ 'progress' ክኸዱ ኣይኽእሉን። 'Some' ግን ምስ ክልቲኦም ስለ ዝኸይድ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option C እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The police ________ investigating the robbery that occurred near the national bank.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
'Police' is a collective noun that is grammatically plural and always takes a plural verb.

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Because 'police' does not end in '-s', many non-native speakers mistake it for a singular noun and pair it with singular verbs like 'is' or 'was'. This is a highly targeted agreement trap in the national exam.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'Police' (ፖሊስ) ዝብል ስም ክትርእዮ ከለኻ ናይ ነጸላ (singular) ይመስል እምበር፡ ብሰዋስው ግን ወትሩ ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ (plural) ተገይሩ ስለ ዝውሰድ ድሕሪኡ ዝመጽእ ግሲ 'are' (Option B) ክኸውን ኣለዎ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which sentence contains a subordinate clause of reason?

options.A: She liked the story because it was funny.
options.B: She liked the story and laughed.
options.C: She liked the story very much.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** A clause of reason begins with because, since or as.

**Step 2:** "because it was funny" explains why she liked it.

**Step 3:** The others are simple or compound sentences.

**Tip:** Subordinate clauses depend on a main clause and start with words such as because, although, when, if, who, which. Collocations are word pairs that naturally go together (make a decision, heavy rain).

cards.title: Lexical cohesion: collocation
rule: **Collocations** are words that naturally go together: *make a decision, do homework, heavy rain, strong tea, take a photo, pay attention, commit a crime*. Using correct collocations makes writing natural and connects ideas.
Writers also link sentences by **repeating** key words and using **synonyms**.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "He did a mistake."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** **Collocations** are words that naturally go together: *make a decision, do homework, heavy rain, strong tea, take a photo, pay attention, commit a crime*. Using correct collocations makes writing natural and connects ideas.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "He did a mistake." breaks this rule.
**Check:** Writers also link sentences by **repeating** key words and using **synonyms**.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: **MAKE** creates something new (a decision, a plan); **DO** carries out a task (homework, the dishes).

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Subordinate clauses depend on a main clause and start with subordinators of time, reason, contrast, condition and purpose; use a comma when they come first. Collocations are natural word partners such as make a decision and do homework.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the natural collocation: "The teacher asked us to ____ attention."
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "pay attention" is the fixed collocation.

**Step 2:** "give attention" is rare and not the normal expression.

**Step 3:** "make" and "do" do not collocate with attention.

**Tip:** Subordinate clauses depend on a main clause and start with words such as because, although, when, if, who, which. Collocations are word pairs that naturally go together (make a decision, heavy rain).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which phrase is a correct collocation?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "strong" collocates with coffee and tea.

**Step 2:** "powerful" collocates with engines or arguments.

**Step 3:** "heavy" and "mighty" are not natural with coffee.

**Tip:** Subordinate clauses depend on a main clause and start with words such as because, although, when, if, who, which. Collocations are word pairs that naturally go together (make a decision, heavy rain).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the best word: "The book received ____ praise from critics."
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "high praise" is the natural collocation.

**Step 2:** "tall" is used for height of people and buildings.

**Step 3:** "big praise" and "upward praise" are not natural.

**Tip:** Subordinate clauses depend on a main clause and start with words such as because, although, when, if, who, which. Collocations are word pairs that naturally go together (make a decision, heavy rain).
